title: An unbreakable secret
subtitle: Quantum cryptography with the BB84 protocol: a spy can't listen in without leaving footprints.

steps.title: Alice, Bob and Eve
body: Alice wants to agree on a secret key with Bob. Eve, the spy, listens to everything. On a classical line, Eve can copy the bits without leaving a trace.
In 1984, Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard proposed using qubits. Since measuring changes the state, any eavesdropping leaves marks. That's BB84.

steps.title: Two bases
body: Alice encodes each bit in one of two “bases”, chosen at random. In the + basis, she uses |0⟩ and |1⟩. In the × basis, she uses |+⟩ and |−⟩.
Bob also picks a basis at random to measure in. Measuring in the × basis is the same as applying an H and then measuring normally.

steps.title: Bob picks the wrong basis
steps.body: Alice sends |+⟩ (bit 0 in the × basis). Bob measures in the + basis.
steps.after: A random result: Bob's bit says nothing about Alice's.

steps.title: Bob picks the right basis
steps.body: Same |+⟩, but now Bob measures in the × basis (an H before measuring).
steps.after: Always 0 — Alice's bit. Afterwards, the two announce publicly only the bases they used (never the bits) and throw away the rounds where the bases didn't match. What's left is the key.

steps.question: Eve intercepts the |+⟩ photon and measures in the + basis (here, she “writes down” the result in her own qubit with a CNOT). Bob then measures in the right basis, ×. What's the chance Bob gets the wrong bit (1)?
steps.explain: 50%! Eve's measurement destroyed the superposition. Since Eve only picks the wrong basis half the time, on average she introduces about 25% errors in the bits that should match. Alice and Bob compare a sample of the key: if the error rate is high, they know they've been spied on.

steps.question: Why doesn't Eve just copy the photon, let the original go on and measure only the copy?

options.why: It's not about cost: it's impossible, by a law of physics.

options.text: Because of the no-cloning theorem: you can't copy an unknown quantum state.
options.why: Right. If cloning were possible, BB84 (and a lot more) would fall apart. The linearity of quantum mechanics forbids it.

options.text: Because the photon explodes if it's copied.
options.why: Nothing that dramatic — the copy simply can't be made faithfully.

steps.title: A quantum video call
steps.text: In 2017, the Micius satellite distributed quantum keys between stations in China and Austria, which were used to encrypt an intercontinental video conference between Beijing and Vienna.
steps.source: Liao et al., Physical Review Letters (2018).

takeaways: In BB84, Alice and Bob pick bases at random and keep only the bits where their bases match.
Measuring in the wrong basis gives random results — and spying shows up as errors.
The no-cloning theorem stops Eve from copying the qubits without being noticed.
